lesson.title: Voltage Gain and the Decibel: Measuring Amplification
lesson.summary: Voltage gain is the ratio of a circuit's output voltage to its input voltage, and when expressed in decibels using 20 log10 of that ratio, it becomes the standard way engineers describe how much an amplifier boosts a signal.
lesson.body:
Voltage gain, usually written Av, is defined as the ratio of a circuit's output voltage to its input voltage: Av = Vout divided by Vin. A gain of 1 means the output equals the input, a gain greater than 1 means the circuit amplifies the signal, and a gain less than 1 means the circuit attenuates it. Because voltage gain can range from tiny fractions to many thousands depending on the circuit, engineers usually convert it into decibels, using Av in dB = 20 times log10(Vout divided by Vin). The factor of 20, rather than 10, comes directly from the definition of the decibel as a power ratio: since power delivered to a fixed resistance is proportional to voltage squared, 10 times log10 of the ratio squared simplifies to 20 times log10 of the ratio, which is why voltage, and current, ratios use 20 while power ratios use 10 in front of the logarithm.

Consider an amplifier stage with an input signal of 10 millivolts, 0.01 V, and an output signal of 2 volts. The voltage gain as a plain ratio is Av = 2 divided by 0.01 = 200. Converting to decibels: Av in dB = 20 times log10(200). Since log10(200) = log10(2) + log10(100) = 0.301 + 2 = 2.301, the gain in decibels is 20 times 2.301 = 46.02 dB. So a plain ratio of 200 corresponds to about 46 dB of voltage gain. As a sanity check, every factor of 10 in voltage ratio adds 20 dB, since log10(10) = 1, so 200 sits a little above the two decade mark of 40 dB, and the extra factor of 2 in the ratio accounts for the additional 6.02 dB, bringing the total to 46.02 dB.

Expressing gain in decibels turns multiplication into addition: if one amplifier stage provides 20 dB of voltage gain and a second stage in series provides another 26 dB, the combined gain is simply 20 + 26 = 46 dB, the exact figure calculated above for a single stage with a ratio of 200, without ever having to multiply the two stages' voltage ratios together directly. That additive property is the main reason decibels, built on the logarithm introduced with the decibel concept, are the standard unit for describing gain throughout audio and RF electronics.
